newsitem.title: USA: IMF board agrees on need for debt relief for Uganda.
newsitem.headline: IMF board agrees on need for debt relief for Uganda.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday gave its stamp of approval for a debt relief plan for Uganda, making it the first candidate of a new international initiative to help the poorest countries.

Monetary sources said the IMF decision to move ahead with the plan followed a similar move by the World Bank on Monday and could eventually lead to a reduction in the country's debt by about $385 million. Uganda has about $3.4 billion in international debt.
"There was a consensus to go ahead on Uganda," World Bank officials told a briefing after the IMF deliberations, adding that work has also begun on choosing additional countries.

One sticking point on Uganda was when to allow the deal to be completed with some countries suggesting it should be very soon, while others, including the United States, recommending it take place in April 1999.

The sources, however, said there seemed to be a growing consensus that the deal, the first under the heavily indebted poor countries debt initiative, should occur between April and November of next year.

This and other matters involving the assistance for Uganda would be hammered out in upcoming discussions between the multilateral banks and other creditors, including the Paris Club with the final decision likely in late April or early May.

Uganda has made great strides in recent years to reform its economy and was identified early on as a candidate for the ambitious new program to help the poorest countries reduce their debt load to levels they can handle.
But the United States has argued it would like to see Uganda continue along the path of reform for some time after the commitment of relief was made to make certain it will not lose its way.

In general, a country is required under the initiative to establish a six-year record with IMF tutorship that shows strong economic reform efforts, although substantial flexibility is provided on a case by case basis.

The initiative was undertaken when it became clear that repayment of old loans to lending agencies such as the World Bank and IMF were draining some of the poorest countries, making it impossible for them to get on their feet no matter what reform efforts they made.
In the briefing, World Bank officials said a number of other countries had been identified as likely candidates to follow Uganda including Bolivia, Mozambique, Burkina Faso and the Ivory Coast.

"We did the preliminary analysis for a few other countries in Latin American as well as Africa and basically we are going to circulate those documents shortly to our board with a view to have them discussed, I guess in the first half of April," a Bank official told reporters.
